prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- German zookeepers in Nuremberg will bottle-feed a four-week-old polar bear and rear it away from its mother after concerns the mother would eat her cub, officials said Thursday. Zookeepers fear the unnamed polar bear cub could be at risk of being eaten. The cub, which doesn't yet have a name, was being cared for at Nuremberg City Zoo, where it was resting under heat lamps and is drinking formula. "It's gaining weight, it's very hungry, it drinks a lot of milk," said Alexandra Foghammar, a spokeswoman for the city. The zoo announced Thursday that the cub is female. Wednesday, the zoo said keepers decided to take the cub away from its mother, Vera, because the mother was showing signs of being upset and confused, taking her baby in and out of the animals' enclosure. "We were 100 percent sure that the baby was going to die if we didn't take it away from her," Nuremberg zoo director Dag Encke told Time magazine. "This would have been a death verdict for the cub." The zoo confirmed earlier this week that its other female polar bear, Vilma, had eaten her two offspring. The zoo said it feared Vera would do the same, so it took her cub away as a precaution. Since then, the cub is thriving in the care of humans, but Vera seems to miss her cub, Foghammar said.  Watch how zoo has faced criticism over polar bears. » . "The mother is a little bit nervous," she said. "She walks around and is searching for the baby, but the responsible persons for the zoo say this is normal. It will continue for three or four days. It's a normal situation." The zookeepers are pondering whether to bring another adult bear, possibly the cub's father, Felix, to the zoo to help Vera overcome her loss, and are seeking another small bear to serve as a companion for the rescued cub, Time reported. The zoo said a keeper entered Vilma's enclosure Monday and noticed that her two cubs were nowhere to be found. The zoo said it assumes Vilma ate her young because she believed the cubs were sick, though zookeepers say the cubs were last seen on Sunday and appeared in good health. But Foghammar told Time that the separation of the bears was bad for the "principle of wildlife conservation" at the zoo: "Now the cub will not grow up to act in a natural way, just as the mother lacked the experience to bring up a cub." The plight of the cub follows the case last year of Knut, a cub rejected by its mother at Berlin Zoo who became the focus of a media frenzy after animal rights campaigners called for it to be killed, claiming it had become too dependent on humans. The unnamed cub is being cared for at Nuremberg City Zoo, where she is resting under heat lamps and drinking formula.

The zoo announced Thursday that the cub is female. On Wednesday, officials said keepers had decided to separate her from her mother, Vera, after Vera showed signs of distress and confusion, repeatedly carrying her cub in and out of the animals’ enclosure.

Earlier this week, the zoo confirmed that its other female polar bear, Vilma, had eaten her two offspring. Fearing Vera might do the same, officials removed her cub as a precaution.

Since then, the cub has thrived in human care, although Vera appears to miss her, Foghammar said.

“The mother is a little bit nervous,” she said. “She walks around and is searching for the baby, but the responsible persons for the zoo say this is normal. It will continue for three or four days. It’s a normal situation.”

Zookeepers are considering bringing another adult bear—possibly the cub’s father, Felix—to the zoo to help Vera overcome her loss. They are also searching for another small bear to serve as a companion for the rescued cub, *Time* reported.

(CNN) — Zoo staff in Nuremberg, Germany, plan to hand-raise and bottle-feed a four-week-old polar bear separately from its mother because they feared she might eat the cub, officials said Thursday.

The unnamed female cub is being looked after at Nuremberg City Zoo, where she rests beneath heat lamps and drinks formula. City spokeswoman Alexandra Foghammar said the young bear has a strong appetite, consumes plenty of milk and is putting on weight. The zoo confirmed Thursday that the cub is female.

On Wednesday, officials announced that keepers had removed the cub from her mother, Vera. They said Vera appeared distressed and disoriented and repeatedly carried her baby into and out of the enclosure. Zoo director Dag Encke told *Time* magazine that staff were completely certain the cub would die if they did not intervene, describing the decision to leave her with Vera as effectively a death sentence.

Earlier in the week, the zoo confirmed that another female polar bear, Vilma, had eaten her two cubs. Concerned that Vera might behave similarly, staff separated her from her offspring as a preventive measure.

The cub has since done well under human care, though Vera appears to be looking for her, Foghammar said. The mother is somewhat anxious and walks around searching for the cub, but zoo officials consider that response normal and expect it to last three or four days.

The zoo has faced criticism over its handling of the polar bears. According to *Time*, keepers are considering bringing in another adult bear—possibly Felix, the cub’s father—to help Vera adjust to the loss. They are also searching for another young bear that could become a companion for the rescued cub.

On Monday, a keeper entered Vilma’s enclosure and discovered that her two cubs had disappeared. Zoo officials believe Vilma ate them because she thought they were ill, although staff said the cubs had appeared healthy when they were last seen Sunday.

Foghammar told *Time* that separating the bears conflicts with the zoo’s wildlife-conservation principles. She explained that the cub will now be deprived of a natural upbringing, just as Vera lacked the experience needed to raise a cub herself.

The situation recalls the previous year’s case of Knut, a polar bear cub rejected by his mother at Berlin Zoo. Knut became the center of intense media attention after animal-rights activists argued that he should be killed because he had grown overly reliant on humans.
